metadata.title: A Car Turning at Constant Speed Is Still Accelerating
metadata.register: formal, undergrad/grad audience, no casual narration, no doodle asides
metadata.branding: none — unbranded, book content only, no channel/logo/handle

beats.narration_text: You're driving at a perfectly steady sixty kilometers per hour around a curve. Are you accelerating?
beats.new_visual_element: Short-only question card: the driving question appears centered on screen in ink text with a crimson underline, posed before any explanation begins.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: question card faded out, blank cream background

beats.narration_text: Picture yourself driving at a perfectly steady sixty kilometers per hour around this curve. Your speedometer never moves. So here is the question: are you accelerating?
beats.new_visual_element: A top-down view of a curved road in ink on white. A teal rectangle, the car, sits at the start of the curve. A speed readout in the corner reads 60 km/h and stays fixed throughout.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: car at rest at the start of the curved road, speed readout visible

beats.narration_text: Watch the velocity arrow as the car moves along the curve. Its length, which represents the speed, never changes. Its direction, however, keeps swinging as the car turns.
beats.new_visual_element: The car travels along the curved road at constant speed. A crimson arrow labeled v, always tangent to the curve, moves with it. Three faded copies of this arrow remain along the path at earlier positions, all the same length, each pointing a different direction.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: car partway along the curve, live tangent arrow v in crimson, three faded snapshot arrows along the path behind it

beats.narration_text: Acceleration is defined as the rate of change of the velocity vector, not the rate of change of speed. Two velocity vectors with the same length but different directions still represent a change, and that change is what we call delta v.
beats.new_visual_element: Two of the faded velocity arrows are brought to a shared origin, tails together. A crimson arrow connecting their tips is labeled delta v. The equation a equals delta v over delta t appears beside it.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: two velocity arrows at a common tail point, delta v arrow between their tips, equation a equals delta v over delta t visible

beats.narration_text: That change in direction points toward the inside of the curve. This inward-pointing acceleration is called centripetal acceleration, and it exists even though the speedometer never moved.
beats.new_visual_element: Back on the curved road, the car continues at constant speed. The crimson tangent arrow v remains, and a new slate arrow labeled a is drawn perpendicular to it, pointing toward the inside of the curve. Both arrows rotate together, staying perpendicular, as the car advances.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: car on the curve with both v (crimson, tangent) and a (slate, inward) arrows attached, rotating together

beats.narration_text: A steady speed does not mean zero acceleration. If the direction of motion is changing, the velocity vector is changing, and that is all acceleration ever means.
beats.new_visual_element: The car freezes mid-curve, with the crimson v arrow and slate a arrow both held in place and labeled. A gold-highlighted line of text beneath reads: constant speed, changing direction, still accelerating.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: final held frame: car mid-curve, v and a arrows held, gold-highlighted punchline text beneath
